title: Linear-seed hardness-to-randomness sampling
formal:
Does there exist one explicit family of point samplers
\[H_{\ell,s}:\{0,1\}^{d(\ell,s)}\to(\{0,1\}^{\ell})^{m(\ell,s)}\]
and absolute constants \(C\ge1\) and rational \(\beta\in(0,1)\) with the following property for every pair of integers \(\ell\ge1\), \(s\ge2\)? The lengths obey
\[d(\ell,s)\le C\ell,\qquad \max\{1,\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\}\le m(\ell,s)\le s.\]
For every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{\ell}\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying
\[\forall B\text{ of size at most }s,\quad\Pr_{x\sim U_{\ell}}[B(x)=f(x)]\le\tfrac12+\tfrac1s,\]
form the \(m\)-bit generator
\[G_f(z)=f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_1)\,f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_2)\cdots f(H_{\ell,s}(z)_m).\]
Must it then satisfy
\[\forall D\text{ of size at most }m,\quad\bigl|\Pr_{z\sim U_d}[D(G_f(z))=1]-\Pr_{u\sim U_m}[D(u)=1]\bigr|\le1/m?\]
The circuits, explicitness and probability spaces are defined below. The sampler is chosen independently of \(f\); each output bit of \(G_f\) is exactly one evaluation of \(f\) at the corresponding sampled point.
why: This asks whether strong average-case hardness can be converted into many pseudorandom bits while using a seed only a constant factor longer than one input to the hard function, and preserving an especially simple evaluation form. Such a result would make the hardness-to-randomness connection more modular and usable across different computational classes. The restriction concerns the structure of the transformation, not merely the final existence of a short-seed generator.
status_note: Open Problem 7.25, its surrounding Nisan–Wigderson parameter analysis and the source’s comparison with general generators were read on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-literature search and comparison with the 2022 nearly optimal generator theorem found no resolution of the exact sampled-evaluation transformation under ordinary average-case circuit hardness. This is a dated source-open target with a bounded later check.

progress.text: The Nisan–Wigderson construction establishes the point-evaluation paradigm; the source presents its quantitative seed and hardness guarantees in Theorems 7.19 and 7.24.
Open Problem 7.25 explicitly asks for linear seed length and polynomially many pseudorandom output bits while preserving the sampled-evaluation form.

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman publish nearly optimal quantitative generators under stronger randomized nondeterministic circuit-hardness assumptions and using a different transformation structure.

sentences: A hard Boolean function can provide pseudorandom bits by being evaluated at carefully correlated inputs.
The question asks for a uniform sampler using only a constant multiple of one input length as its random seed.
It must produce polynomially many bits in the hardness parameter, each from exactly one evaluation of the original function.
Every function with the specified average-case circuit hardness must yield a generator fooling the stated circuits to inverse-output-length error.
General short-seed transformations and newer results under stronger hardness assumptions do not automatically preserve this required evaluation form.

definitions:
\(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on \(t\)-bit strings. The probabilities in the premise and conclusion use fresh independent uniform strings of the indicated lengths. They are computational distinguishability guarantees, not statistical closeness against unbounded tests.

A Boolean circuit is a finite acyclic graph with input wires, free Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and one output wire. Size counts computation gates, including NOT gates, but not input wires or constants. The circuits \(B\) and \(D\) are deterministic and completely nonuniform; \(B\) has \(\ell\) inputs and \(D\) has \(m\). Their choices may depend on all parameters and on \(f\). They have no oracle access to \(f\). Allowing additional independent random input wires does not change these guarantees, because fixing the random bits gives a deterministic circuit of no greater size and averaging preserves the displayed inequalities. The premise means that even the best size-\(s\) predictor has advantage at most \(1/s\) over a fair guess.

Explicitness is uniform deterministic polynomial-time computation of the sampler. There are fixed multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\) such that the parameter machine on \((1^{\ell},s)\), with \(s\) binary, outputs integer lengths \(d,m\), and the evaluation machine on \((1^{\ell},s,z)\) writes the ordered list of all \(m\) sampled \(\ell\)-bit strings. Each runs in at most \(K(\ell+s+1)^q\) steps on valid inputs. Equivalently the time can be polynomial in \(\ell+m\), because of the polynomial relationship between \(s\) and \(m\). All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, hard-function description or hard-function truth table available to these machines.

The constants and the machines precede the parameters, and \(H_{\ell,s}\) precedes the universal quantifier over \(f\). The family must be computed even for parameter pairs at which no function satisfies the hardness premise; its implication is then vacuous. No algorithm recognizing hard functions is required. The function \(f\) need not itself be efficiently computable: this is a transformation guarantee conditional on its finite-length circuit hardness, not a claim that such hard functions have been constructed. When \(f\) is also computable within a suitable exponential-time bound, the transformation has the usual derandomization applications.

The normalization \(m\le s\) and the lower bound using \(\lfloor s^{\beta}\rfloor\) express the source's polynomially many output bits. A larger qualifying output can be truncated, and fixed multiplicative factors in a polynomial lower bound can be absorbed by reducing \(\beta\) and handling finitely many small hardness parameters. The single-evaluation requirement excludes encoding or otherwise transforming the truth table of \(f\) before producing the output bits.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated sampler-family claim. A positive proof must supply the uniform sampler and constants and establish the implication for every promised \(f\), including the linear seed bound, polynomial output length and size-\(m\), error-\(1/m\) guarantee. A negative proof must rule out all such families, not merely one combinatorial-design construction or one kind of security reduction. A general hardness-to-randomness generator that encodes the hard function or combines several evaluations per output bit does not answer this sampling question.

context_blocks.text: The Nisan–Wigderson construction evaluates the hard function at correlated points determined by a combinatorial design. The source obtains a seed bound of order \(\ell^2/\log s\) while keeping polynomially many output bits. This is linear in \(\ell\) when \(s\) is exponential in \(\ell\), but not throughout the lower-hardness range.

General hardness-to-randomness constructions already improve the seed dependence to linear in the relevant hard-function input length. Vadhan explains that their output bits can depend on an encoding of the entire hard function. Open Problem 7.25 asks for the more restrictive point-evaluation form written here, so those results do not directly settle it.

The 2022 Doron–Moshkovitz–Oh–Zuckerman theorem refines quantitative derandomization under hardness for randomized single-valued nondeterministic circuits. It uses pseudoentropy and extraction and assumes a different, stronger type of circuit hardness. Its nearly optimal parameters are not a theorem for every ordinary average-case-hard function under the one-evaluation-per-bit requirement.

A lower bound for one construction or for a specified reconstructive proof technique would not refute the semantic existence statement. Conversely, merely assuming that a hard function exists is not the desired answer: the question requires one uniform sampler with the stated implication for every function meeting the premise.
